definition: A vanilla option is a plain option (e.g., one whose underlying asset price can be modeled with a lognormal distribution) that can typically be priced with the Black-Scholes formula. An exotic option is any option that does not meet the assumptions of the Black-Scholes model, i.e., cannot be constructed from simple put and call options.
core_idea: The key distinction between vanilla and exotic options is the assumptions needed to model their price; exotic option formulas typically require more variables, and those variables may not behave the same way as in standard models.
key_points: Exotic option: any option that can't be replicated with standard put or call options / doesn't meet Black-Scholes assumptions.
Vanilla option: a normal option with no special features, usually priced with Black-Scholes.
Spread options are a type of exotic option because they involve two underlying assets.
relationships: Spread options are a specific case of exotic options.
